Question: What is the difference between Schrödinger's equation and Hamilton–Jacobi equation?
Answer: Hamilton-Jacobi is a classical equation. Schrödinger equation is a quantum equation. However, Hamilton-Jacobi equation is a precursor of Schrödinger equation. How Schrödinger equation can be “derived” from Hamilton-Jacobi equation constitutes a train of thoughts connecting geometric optics to wave mechanics. It is a beautiful analogy, albeit quite far-stretched. Incidentally, quite a few books on classical mechanics discuss this aspect of Hamilton-Jacobi equation as a connection toward quantum mechanics. In fact, there is only one book by Indian author J.C. Upadhyaya Classical Mechanics. ( p.214-218) which does this. Upadhyaya writes: “Schrödinger wave equation for particle motion (quantum mechanics) is related to ordinary particle (or classical) mechanics as wave (or physical) optics bears the relation to geometrical (or ray) optics.” Goldstein's treatment is fairly sophisticated in terms of geometric optics. Physicist Moshe Carmeli has a 1979 paper recasting general relativity in Hamilton-Jacobi equation and deriving the Schrödinger-type equation for gravitation! It is a 4-page proof in Nuovo Cimento Journal. It must be remembered that though this looks like quantizing gravity, it does not, due to some mathematical difficulties. Understanding Schrödinger equation in the light of Hamilton-Jacobi theory is a very stimulating exercise.

Question: What is the role of quantum mechanics in quantum cosmology?
Answer: Quantum cosmology has quantum mechanics in it. How? This is encapsulated in the Wheeler-DeWitt equation. This is the wavefunction of the universe! We take a closed universe to study the solution of this equation. The original paper of 1983 by Hartle and Hawking is one of pioneering papers on quantum cosmology. I read this paper few years back. The summary itself is the answer to this question. The steps are simple (though the advanced techniques are hard). Recast general relativity into the Hamiltonian form. This is the formalism of “cutting” spacetime into 3-hypersurface and time. Using the 50 years old trick of lapse and shift functions, we get Hamiltonian general relativity. Now quantum mechanics enters here. I reiterate: we have a finite dimensional manifold called minisuperspace to study the solutions though the Wheeler-DeWitt equation applies to an infinite dimensional manifold. To this Hamiltonian we add Dirac quantization to the constraints that arise in the Hamiltonian formalism. The solutions are the functionals of the cosmological constant α . Accordingly, we get different cosmological models. Boundary conditions are important. This equation tells that the universe does not evolve in time! Hawking tells us that the ground state of the universe should be the cosmological analog of a quantum mechanical ground state. This is geometrically stated in a sophisticated manner: the lower half of the 3-sphere is joined to the 4-dimensional anti-deSitter space which is embedded in 5-Minkowksi spacetime! This is a very interesting paper. Everyone interested in cosmology must read this paper. For me, the paper is very difficult to digest as I'm not conversant with advanced Lorentzian geometry. I don't say anything about loop quantum cosmology. I also don't say about particle physics aspect in cosmology which is very important in particle creation. Even after 40 years, this stands as one the finest papers on cosmology. As an aside, Hawking visited Hartle to study path-integrals as applied to cosmology. Hawking studied the tools from Hartle. Hartle was at California then and a leading expert on path-integrals. Stephen Hawking studied the tools with such zest and dedication that he surpassed Hartle in the mathematical machinery required. Hartle admitted: Hawking has more command on path-integrals than I have! The two then “solved” the wavefunction of the universe in the path-integral formalism using the steepest descent method or the saddle point approximation. It is this method which creates different solutions depending upon the cosmology constant. This all appears in the paper. I'm still incompetent to fully understand this interesting paper.

Question: "Quantum" gravity is gravity on the Planck scale?
Answer: Generally, this is the basic requirement to define quantum gravity, simply because the Planck scale displays discrete properties of a classical spacetime (atleast this is what I'm given to understand). Quantum gravity is a difficult subject and different approaches give different viewpoints. Noncommutative geometry expresses quantum gravity in terms of a spectral triple, which is a machinery acting on a non-commutative manifold. The properties of this manifold (non-commutativity of its coordinates) are encapsulated in the spectral triple. So, Connes emphasizes the non-commutativity property more than the Planck scale, although Planck scale is unavoidable in this approach. Perturbative quantum gravity emphasizes the non-renormalizability property of the Feynman diagrams in quantum gravity. So, renormalization plays the role of a key requirement. Penrose's twistor space is where the classical space time is mapped into. This twistor space is then quantized using what are called Kodaira curves. (ideas from algebraic geometry which he learned from Atiyah). But it requires the full Einstein equations to be solved for a general spacetime which Penrose did not succeed in. And nobody till today! I didn't find Planck scale in his exposition. Loop quantum gravity cannot promote certain observables to operators, the hindrance being the Hamiltonian constant. Although LQG succeeds in discrete area operator in terms of Planck scale, the constraint algebra puts further difficulty in quantization of gravity. Here, Dirac first class constraints seem to be the deciding factor. String theory cannot merge its ingredients into the M-theory. Here the definition is about the string vibrations corresponding to different particles. Robert Wald in his influential book General Relativity tells us one property of quantum mechanics: superposition and expectation values. He says if we take expectation values of the energy-momentum tensor, we must take the expectation values of the Einstein tensor too. This would mean, roughly, one half of the time the spacetime would be in configuration M 1 , and the other time it would be in configuration M 2 ! This does not look physically viable. Therefore, one cannot quantize Einstein field equations directly. In a nutshell, there are several quantum properties which physicists and mathematicians take as a starting point to put gravity in that “mould”, while formulating a quantum theory of gravity. Whether all these properties are equivalent for gravitation is something I do not know!

Question: What do you think about the Russian mathematician Grigory Perelman, the author of the proof of the Poincaré conjecture and the Thurston conjecture, who refused all prizes?
Answer: Few days back I wrote an answer as to who was the greatest living mathematician in the world. I mentioned Serre. Though it garnered 67000 views and 223 upvotes, some Quorans trolled me. They did not get my point. There is a difference between a greatest mathematician and a finest mathematician. Mathematical community is like a family. It has its own idols revered by its members for their lifelong sacrifice and contribution, just similar to the feeling we have toward our living grandfather who built the house and kept the household together. Serre is such a “living” mathematician. He is a grandfather figure to today's mathematicians and there is nobody who would downplay his contribution spanning 70+ years! Some put Tao before Serre. Tao is one the finest mathematicians today but certainly not the greatest in terms of his lifetime achievements because he himself is pretty young and looking at his age, he has a long way to go. (Is he an Abel Prize winner?) I reiterated then, that greatest doesn't mean knowing much mathematics. It means creating a culture of its own, motivation, mathematical education through books, putting mathematicians busy for several years, encouraging young mathematicians, building up results which are instrumental in solving great problems. Hilbert was such a man before 1950. Not that he knew much mathematics. There were others who rivaled him in knowledge. But he built a culture of mathematics around his university and made it the center of the world in mathematics. He fought with the faculty for Noether against gender discrimination (who did this sort of thing that time?). What a loss if Noether had not taught at Göttingen? Can anyone imagine? He educated several students and was the only mathematician to have more PhD students than anyone else in the world (even surpassing Poincaré). Almost all his students themselves became great world famous mathematicians. Hilbert invited Einstein and Einstein stayed in his house for discussion on general relativity and Hilbert obliged him. This constitutes greatness. Nowhere I'm exaggerating his mathematical competence. Hardy put him at scale 80. Now to Perelman. Perelman was the finest mathematician in the world. I use “was”, because he no longer is a mathematician though he is said to be alive. He was the first mathematician on this planet to qualify for Fields and Clay! Is he greatest? No! Perelman did not contribute to the community after his Fields proof of the Poincaré's conjecture. He disappeared from the scene. His wealth of knowledge has gone waste. Can you compare his contribution to anyone else excluding mathematical competence. There lies the difference between the finest mathematician and the greatest mathematician. There is absolutely no answer to the question: “who is the greatest mathematician?” But someone can reply to the question: “who is the greatest living mathematician today?” And a mathematical community, being a dynamic entity, acts like a family who identifies its current idols and role models and try to emulate them. Michael Atiyah, for example, claimed to prove the RH but he did not prove it. However, the mathematical community didn't express its disappointment or displeasure or skepticism toward his mathematical excellence. He was undeniably one of the greatest (not only finest) mathematical giants of the second half of the 20th century. And every mathematician acknowledged his 60-years excellent work, even if senility might have affected him to the point of embarrassment. Finally, Grisha Perelman was one the finest mathematicians in the world. His pensioner mother would have been utterly proud to see her son on the top of the world to grab the Fields and the Clay. But his ideology was too sharp to despise everything that his talent and fortune presented before him. His work is very original and sophisticated and required several mathematicians to assess his paper. Imagine, how much differential topology, manifold theory and its subdomains like surgery techniques and obstruction theory would have advanced if he had actively continued teaching and research in his later life. But he preferred to stay with his mother on her pension in a small apartment! He is great only in one sense: he insisted that the Prize be shared or given to Hamilton for his original ideas. This shows his magnanimity. To qualify for the term greatest living, one has to live life like Serre, Witten, Deligne, Connes or Misha Gromov. Certainly not like Perelman. However, I hold immense respect for his mathematical capabilities and I exaggerate that Perelman is/was one of the finest mathematicians on this planet.

I assume that most terms are familiar to math students. What is the relation between Teichmüller space and moduli space. Teichmüller space, roughly, is a more fine-grained notion of moduli space. A sphere has no holes. It has genus 0. The Teichmüller space is just a point since there is only one complex structure on it, the Riemann sphere! Now this is just the tip of the iceberg. Teichmüller theory is intimidatingly vast and complex. No wonder that it is generally discussed at research level. It has connections with string theory as well. Question: What is the process for calculating the probability of finding electrons in a specific region using Schrodinger's wave equation?
Answer: This is a fine question. Ask for a potential V ( x , t ) in which your particle moves. Assume it is independent of time t . So, it becomes V ( x ) .Take your starting wavefunction Ψ ( x , 0 ) . Our job is to get the wavefunction Ψ ( x , t ) for any subsequent time t . To achieve this, we solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. You get, in general, an infinite set of solutions ( ψ 1 ( x ) , ψ 2 ( x ) , ψ 3 ( x ) . . . . ) . Each has its own energy, say, E 1 , E 2 , E 3 , . . Now to express Ψ ( x , 0 ) we consider the general linear combination of these solutions which equals our Ψ ( x , 0 ) . Ψ ( x , 0 ) = ∑ n = ∞ n = 1 c n ψ n ( x ) . Why we do this? Because, we can match the initial state by the correct choice of the constants c 1 , c 2 , c 3 , . . . Now you want the wavefunction Ψ ( x , t ) at a later time t . You just tack onto each term its characteristic time dependence e x p ( − i E n t / ℏ ) . The separable solutions are, Ψ n ( x , t ) = ψ n ( x ) e − i E n t / ℏ Calculate | Ψ | 2 . I have omitted many details such as the method of solving the Schrödinger equation, stationary states, probabilities and expectation values independent of time, etc. Consult the following relatively unknown Schaum book for introductory quantum mechanics. Good luck.

Question: Can you give an example of a connected differentiable manifold whose differentiable structure does not admit a compatible atlas with only a finite number of charts?
Answer: I think the long line is the differentiable manifold which fulfills the conditions given in the question. What is a long line? It is a topological space that is “longer” than a real line. It is denoted by L in some sources. Roughly, it is constructed by taking a collection of open intervals in the real line and arranging them in a linear order without any endpoint. This results in a line that has no endpoints but is longer than the standard real line. Technically, it is the set of all points ( ( x , y ) ) , where ( x ) is a real number, and ( y ) is an element of the interval ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) , equipped with a lexicographic order. Because of the existence of the open intervals, the long line is non-compact. Going into deeper understanding of the concept of long line, we get to know that it is one of the most interesting constructions in general topology. However, very few general books on topology describe the long line. Munkres book Topology includes long line in the exercise section (p.159). I did not find long line in Dugundji's Topology, which is one of the earliest and rigorous sources on topology. It is described in greater detail in the following influential book. Answer: A tricky question! Going by the question, it would imply that Einstein's gravity can be derived from quantum mechanics! We talk only about quantum gravity and leave aside the unified field theory. What things are missing depend upon which route you take to effect quantization of gravity. Some missing items are mathematical, some are conceptual. The question is phrased as telling us that classical mechanics is a “subset” of quantum mechanics which is true in a sense. In this picture, the concept of Hopf algebras or quantum groups comes to my mind. Quantum groups generalize classical groups. They have a very rich algebraic structure of unit, counit, product, coproduct, and many more interesting features. Very roughly, some such Hopf algebras house both classical mechanics and quantum mechanics “simultaneously” depending upon the parameter h . This h acts like a “knob”. This knob, at one end, starts with (the world of) quantum mechanics and turning the knob at the other end lands up in general relativity! Therefore, this Hopf algebra (Poincarè quantum group) provides an excellent example for the unification of gravity (as spacetime geometry) and quantum mechanics! But wait! This is a “toy model”. Nature is too complicated to obey even the (most difficult) mathematics of Hopf algebras. Missing elements are those which fail to accommodate themselves in this structure. Second, in Wald's influential book General Relativity, he gives us a logical flaw arising in the quantum version of Einstein's field equations G = 8 π T . He asks to take expectation values of both sides of the equation after promoting them to operators. This will ensue probabilistic attribute to ^ T and ^ G . For ^ T , this is fine. You have 1/2 probability of getting matter in some spacetime region O 1 and half in O 2 . But for ^ G this is troublesome. You will have discontinuous spacetime curvature, with 1/2 probability of gravitational field in O 1 and other half in O 2 ! This is ridiculous. Whichever route you take, there are missing links. I handpicked these examples because the physical ideas are easy to comprehend. Carlo Rovelli discusses the origin of these missing links to Bronstein's (1936) paper discussing as to why fundamentally classical gravity doesn't fit into the scheme of quantum geometry. Question: What do you think of Roy Kerr's recent paper that rotating black holes may not have a singularity?
Answer: I have not read Kerr's paper. Even if I start reading it, I might not understand the full contents. That being said, let us put Penrose and Kerr together for a debate and see who wins! Nearly 25 years back, we had a book describing the debate between Hawking and Penrose. Now, this is a mathematical debate between Penrose and Hawking and the book has Atiyah's preface. Who wins finally? Nobody! Penrose plays Einstein and Hawking plays Bohr (by Atiyah's own description). The book is very much mathematical. Both physicists argue in terms of sophisticated geometry of Lorentz manifolds, Wheeler-DeWitt equation, Penrose diagrams, naked singularity, Cauchy development, etc. If Atiyah warns us that it is a debate, then why none of the two comes out winner? Reason? The subject is too speculative, albeit dressed in a highly mathematical style. Murray Gell-Mann once got angry with De Witt, “ If you know the wavefunction of the universe, how is that you are not rich still”. Gell-Mann was referring to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation or the Schrödinger equation for the universe! Hawking even solved this equation with advanced differential geometric techniques! So, does it mean the WDW equation describes our universe? No! Now replace Hawking with Kerr. Kerr is a no nonsense theoretical physicist who is 90 now and Penrose is 92! Both dominated general relativity and gravitation in the second half of the 20th century. Kerr is in the league of Penrose, Werner Israel, Stephen Hawking, Kip Thorne, Yakov Zeldovich, etc. Just as Hawking and Penrose had different viewpoints about quantum mechanics and the geometry of singularities, same can be said for the Kerr-Penrose debate. The singularity theorems are not modeled on ordinary mechanics like work-energy theorem, Lami's theorem, Castigliano's theorem, etc. We still don't have a viable theory of quantum gravity. And in its absence, we cannot talk much about presence of singularities, even if Raychaudhari equation for congruence of geodesics is invoked in the Hawking-Penrose singularity theorem. I myself have read the proof of the H-P singularity theorem and found not too difficult to digest if one follows some terminology of the causal structure of spacetime. Is Kerr wrong? I don't think so. Is Penrose wrong? No! Then what is correct? Every piece of mathematics, however elegant and consistent it might be, does not necessarily correspond to reality, which is why nobody wins in the book I described above. If tomorrow loop quantum cosmology attains its position of completeness, consistency, and enjoys empirical support, it might shed light on the entire issue of all arguments surrounding singular spacetimes. Calling a theorem wrong takes much boldness. But some theorems work at an exceptionally high plane of physical and mathematical abstraction, which always leaves a room for skepticism about them. Take, for example, Haag's theorem in quantum field theory. Though it is christened as a theorem, there are several differing opinions about its veracity, limitations, scope, relevance, etc. among the practioners of QFT. This much being said in a broad context, Kerr's arguments which are, in fact, not new are definitely not dismissive. Mathematical results pertaining to theoretical cosmology are prone to skepticism as long as the final theory of quantum gravity is not around! Finally, Hawking himself remarked, “Wait for quantum gravity. Once it arrives, it will smooth out singularities”. Till then it is “childish” to set up quarrel between Kerr and Penrose or to invite Toth to act as a mediator!

Much of initial formalism is the standard material on Hamiltonian mechanics. All we have to deal with are the 4 constraints and 6 evolution equations. The basic idea is to turn constraints into operators. Most importantly, we obtain the area operator with discrete spectrum. LQG has a familiar mathematical formalism. I haven't seen algebraic topology, homological algebra, homotopy, algebraic geometry, etc. being used in LQG, atleast not upto Thiemann's spin-network papers. String theory is an “octopus”. Just as Kaluza-Klein theory was revived 50 years later giving rise to strings, and forming chief inspiration for it, strings may be revived after few decades in something different yet to come.

Question: What is the most difficult topic in real and complex analysis, and how do you deal with it?
Answer: If you read papa Rudin, you will appreciate the “geography” of difficult topics in real and complex analysis. Ahlfors’ Complex Analysis will also do. The term most difficult is to be interpreted with respect to who is asking about it: student, graduate student, professor, international figure working in the field, and so on. Again, if you ask me, I would mention monodromy theorem, Picard Big theorem, Hurwitz theorem, and many such results which are extremely beautiful and mysterious in their statements, but employ techniques far advanced. But this is just the beginning. We go to several complex variables which is a very “complex” extension of single variable complex analysis. Several complex variables starts with Hartog’s extension theorem and immediately progresses to results of extreme depth and complexity (Weierstrass preparation theorem). In another direction you come across complex manifolds and complex structures which use complex geometry (this is again a vast field in complex analysis). You often hear Newlander-Nirenberg theorem, Kähler manifolds, Fubini-Study metric in this region. Go further and you see marriage of algebraic geometry and complex analysis in the form of thousands of deep results: Jacobian of curve, Torelli theorem, Kodaira vanishing theorem, Kodaira embedding theorem, Riemann-Roch theorem and its several generalizations. Where to stop? Which is the most difficult topic? Nobody can answer precisely. The entire complex algebraic geometry gone into studying the Hodge conjecture is too vast to be in any one single person's intellectual capacity! Same may be true for the Riemann hypothesis. Generally, I avoid answering questions about asking which is the most difficult topic in any given subject. The set of most difficult topics on any given subject is not well-ordered, speaking in the language of Zermelo's well-ordering theorem!

Name: Rajratna Adsul
Question: What are your thoughts on professors who ask questions during lecture and then don't answer them themselves? Do you think it's OK or not OK? Why or why not?
Answer: This is a good sign. In my days, some professors used to ask questions just to make sure that students don't doze off. This is important to make the whole class an interactive session. In my case (as a student), I used to be cautious about the topic and prepare myself a bit, with the thought that “this man would make me stand up and ask questions. So I better be attentive to the fullest”. (It is not that I was not a serious student. But this was just to avoid making laughing stock of myself in case I fumble). Once students know the pedagogical style of their teacher or professor, they orient themselves. On the other hand, some students are extra-smart. They would shoot a question in the middle of the lecture to clarify a certain point. If the professor cannot clarify the doubt on the spot, he would assure the student to resolve the point after the lecture or something like that. (Pauli once interrupted Einstein's lecture telling the nearby attendees that Einstein's point of topic was not so stupid as they had thought before). If a professor asks a question and does not answer himself, it means he just wants to make you attentive to his lecture. This is one reason. Another reason is just to make you curious about the question, whose answer is not expected to know at that point of time, which would be a digression. For example, while discussing Lagrange's equations from D'Alembert's principle, my professor asked one of us, “Is it fine if we take one-one correspondence between Cartesian coordinates and generalized coordinates to solve the virtual work done by D'Alembert's principle?”. The class was silent. He continued, “ OK, I shall tell you when we come to that part of the derivation when it is needed”. And he did explain it. Incidentally, the derivation of Euler-Lagrange's equations from D'Alembert's principle is one of the longest derivations in classical mechanics! Goldstein takes 6 pages (Classical Mechanics p.16 to 21) in introducing D'Alembert's principle and proceeding to the derivation! Some professors would intimidate students with sophisticated questions whose answers might not be known to them. Finally, everything is OK when you have understood what your professor has taught you. I often ask my students one beautiful question from Resnick-Halliday (1968): “How can the predictions of wave mechanics be so exact if the only information we have about the positions of the electrons is statistical?” (Physics Part 2, p.1213). They ask me for the answer. I refuse to answer, telling them to find it out by themselves by studying the basic principles of quantum mechanics. Because, the answer to the question enlightens the student after having assimilated the core ideas of quantum theory. Hope this helps!!

Question: How difficult is it to read and understand "complex analysis" by Ahlfors?
Answer: Ahlfors’ book is difficult and generally recommended for advanced graduates and research people. This book is very formal, rigorous and borders around researchful exposition. Though its contents look quite familiar, the material presented is quite advanced and sophisticated in style. Ahlfors is to complex analysis what Rudin is to real analysis! Incidentally, Ahlfors research was related to complex variables which fetched him the Fields Medal. He was also the first to receive it. I have a habit of “gauging” greatness of a book by looking at its contents and to looking for some sophisticated results if the book discusses the results or not: Hadamard's theorem, Jensen's formula, Picard's theorem, Weierstrass theorem, etc. Weierstrass has several theorems on complex analysis and on topics related to complex variables. In this book, Ahlfors derives Picard's celebrated theorem (using ideas from monodromy theorem and modular functions). Other books on complex analysis avoid the proof of this theorem citing ideas required which the reader does not seem to possess. Ahlfors has no reason to shy away from the proof of Picard's theorem: after all he is writing for researchers! Also Ahlfors explains homology with cycles and chains drawing original idea from Cauchy's theorem. Other books, generally, do not treat connectivity and other topological property in discussing homology by Cauchy's theory. The list goes on. Seldom there arises a book which captures the attention of students and teachers and also researchers for several years, going beyond 5 decades, for its rigor, elegance and masterful exposition. Such a book does inspire “fear”. Nevertheless, students do display courage and tenacity to climb the Mt. Everest of complex analysis which this book by Alhfors represents! Ahlfors once said on his retirement function, “I don't need to publish, because I shall never perish”.

Question: Can I see a proof of Hodge conjecture before I die?
Answer: That's a sharp question! It depends upon your present age. I find it difficult to see the Hodge conjecture being put to rest before 2050. Now that all great algebraic geometers are pretty old: Serre, Deligne, Mumford, Hironaka, Mori, etc. These are some of the brightest minds in mathematics on this planet having expertise in the subject to which the conjecture belongs. Nevertheless, the conjecture is still open! Hilbert imagined that if he were to be reborn after 500 years, the first question he would ask, “Has anyone solved the Riemann hypothesis?” Therefore, he extrapolated 500 years to develop the mathematical artillery enough to tackle the Riemann hypothesis! This is, of course, an overstatement. Alain Connes, one of the Fields Medalists who also worked on Riemann hypothesis, is now “tired” and is pursuing the Standard Model with gravity. I have high hopes from “youngsters” like Tao, Lurie and Scholze to handle this conjecture, even though they are not exactly working in this field. Hodge conjecture is even difficult to state and understand in ordinary language and many books which discuss the Millennium Problems (at popular level) generally don't spend much energy in elucidating this conjecture. This book introduces these problems to the reader in the most down-to-earth manner. Nevertheless, the author has not been successful in the case of Hodge conjecture. Anyway, we are lucky to witness FLT and Poincarè's conjecture being solved finally. The next generation may witness some more conjectures being tackled.

Question: How can we say that external charges do not contribute to any flux through the Gaussian surface? The strength of flux that had entered will not be equal to that of which leaves as it depends on distance from source.Then why do we say so?
Answer: No. Your argument is beautiful, but it is not so. Let E be the flux entering a Gaussian surface due to a point charge q . The Gaussian surface is shown below. On a spherical surface, the normal component E n is just the magnitude of E. Take E as minus at a and plus at b . The magnitude of E decreases as 1 / r 2 , but the surface area is proportional to r 2 . Therefore, the product of flux and surface area is independent of r . The flux entering a is cancelled by the flux out of b . The total flow of flux out of S is zero. A beautiful question in fact! Question: Is it possible to write math expressions in normal human language so that everyone will understand it easily without needing any knowledge of math itself beforehand?
Answer: No. This is not possible. It is, however, possible to interpret certain math expressions in normal human language for someone who has some faint idea of the subject in which the equation under consideration occurs. Richard Feynman did just this. The long math expressions in particle scattering are called the S-matrix elements. It is difficult (though not impossible) to build up the total picture of the process unless you set up a clean and clear dictionary between the term of the S-matrix and a step of the physical process in the scattering. Though contemporary physicists criticized Feynman for his oversimplification of the interpretation of such terms, the Feynman diagrams have come down to us as an indispensable tool in physical interpretation of the quantum processes. An ordinary student of quantum mechanics just needs to know what mathematical term represents which step. This dictionary is the so-called Feynman rules which dominate much of quantum field theory. The ubiquitous use of these pictures called Feynman diagrams has given us the philosophy of interpretation of mathematics in a visualizable way. For example, why is there a Dirac δ − function under the integral which represents some process? Here, the Dirac delta function enforces the conservation of momentum in the process. What does the following expression mean: i q 2 − m 2 ? The above is called a propagator and this term represents the transfer or propagation of momentum from one particle to another. Here q is momentum and m is the mass of the particle in the process. Finally, the integral schematically looks like this: ∫ A B C D d x ∫ Here, A,B,C,D are the math terms in the S-matrix of the process. Each of these A,B,C,D has a physical meaning corresponding to the step of the process. In other words, each symbol has a Feynman diagram. We read the terms from right to left, i.e. from D towards A. It means a particle with property D starts to meet at a point x making some interaction C , then going toward some x ′ to meet someone with some energy B and finally going out to infinity with some property A . This is very rough idea but it renders the flavor. Schwinger and Wheeler objected to Feynman for such a classical depiction of quantum processes. But barring rigor, Feynman gave us this beautiful piece of interplay of mathematical expressions and physical ideas. However, the question asks too much. Question: What is an example of a function whose Taylor's expansion does not exist at all points? Why does this happen?
Answer: One function which is often discussed in this context is f ( x ) = e − 1 / x 2 for x ≠ 0 f ( x ) = 0 for x = 0 This function satisfies the criterion of infinite differentiability at a for Taylor series to exist for f ( x ) at x = a . This function and all its derivatives are continuous in every interval, even at x = 0 , and at this point all the derivatives vanish, that is, f ( n ) ( 0 ) = 0 for every value of n . The Taylor expansion of f ( x ) is, f ( 0 ) + x 1 ! f ′ ( 0 ) + x 2 2 ! f ′′ ( 0 ) + ⋅ ⋅ ⋅ Here all the coefficients of the approximating polynomials P n ( 0 ) vanish, no matter what value is chosen for n . Now why this happens? The remainder here remains equal to the function itself, and thus, except for x = 0 , cannot approach zero as n increases, since the function is positive for every other value of x . Remember, this function tells us that the condition of infinite differentiability is by no means sufficient. The moral of the story: a function for which all derivatives exist and are continuous throughout an interval still need not be capable of expansion in a Taylor series. The remainder R n in Taylor's theorem may fail to tend to zero as n increases, no matter how small the interval is, in which we want to expand the function. The following book (though this example is not discussed in it) shows how functions behave contrary to the expected behavior. This book is awesome in every respect.

Question: What is the reason that in general relativity (GR), the equation of motion for a particle is not independent of the choice of coordinates?
Answer: General relativity has this peculiar property. The equation of motion for a particle is dependent upon the choice of the coordinates, because motion depends upon the metric of the space under consideration. Now metric “properties” change from coordinates to coordinates. Take a flat space. Express its metric in Cartesian and polar coordinates. In Cartesian coordinates, you get Christoffel symbols zero, confirming a flat space. In polar coordinates, you get non-zero Christoffel symbols even if the Riemann curvature tensor is zero here. The laws of physics are not changed, and they are no better or worse in either of the coordinates. You have only the transformation (aka diffeomorphism) between the coordinates which translate the laws of physics from one reference frame to the other. In other words, it is like translating a sentence or a paragraph into a different language. Though the paragraph would look different in two different languages, the inherent meaning of the content remains unchanged, as expected.

Question: Is curvature the exterior covariant derivative of the connection?
Answer: Yes. But this is with reference to the principal fiber bundle P . The curvature 2-form F of the connection is the Lie algebra-valued exterior covariant derivative of the connection 1-form ω . There are few books which explain this concept in an intuitive or clear way. For a flat connection on a trivial bundle, you need just exterior derivative. But for curved surfaces, the exterior derivative is replaced with the covariant exterior derivative. It took a while for me to digest this notion few years back. One surprising property of exterior covariant derivative is that it does not square to zero, unlike the usual exterior derivative ( d 2 = 0 ) . The square of exterior covariant derivative is not zero but proportional to F . Why? John Baez, in his well-written book Gauge Fields, Knots and Gravity, supplies a beautiful answer (p.249). “ This makes sense, because the reason why d 2 vanishes is that partial derivatives ∂ μ commute. But the curvature measures the failure of covariant partials D μ to commute.” Diagrammatically, Ω : Γ ( T 2 0 P ) → L ( G ) . Here Ω is our exterior covariant derivative which “eats” a two-form on a principal tangent bundle and “spits” values in Lie algebra of the structure group G . Ω = D ω is a 2-form on P . Here ω is connection one-form on P .

Question: When deriving the Euler-Lagrange equation, why do we take a Taylor series, and why can we neglect the higher order terms?
Answer: This is not always the route to deriving the Euler-Lagrange equations. Some authors derive the equations from D'Alembert's principle, some from Newton's second law, etc. Take action S . Invoking the principle of least action δ S = 0 , leads us to the equations of motion for the system. To derive Newton's second law, we start with a small change in coordinates given by x → x + ϵ , where ϵ is small. This variation is constrained to keep the end points fixed, ϵ ( t 1 ) = ϵ ( t 2 ) = 0. It is here that we take Taylor's expansion for the potential V ( x ) . V ( x + ϵ ) = V ( x ) + ϵ ∂ V ∂ x . Take your Lagrangian L = 1 2 m ˙ v 2 − V ( x ) . Take action S of L . Vary the action S . We get S = S + δ S . The requirement that δ S = 0 forces us to see that one of the integrals is 0. As end points are arbitrary, the integrand in question must be identically 0. This whole mathematical and physics exercise gives us the following famous Newton's second law. m ¨ x + ∂ V ∂ x = 0 ⇒ m ¨ x = − ∂ V ∂ x . The more general situation proceeds in a way to use total differentials of L . I have omitted the mathematical details of the calculation of δ S = 0 which is a routine calculus exercise. But the particular example above highlights the presence of Taylor's expansion in its earlier stage.

For example, depending upon the relativistic dispersion, we can call the particles massless and the field a massless scalar field. This is a general discussion in the introductory part of QFT. The wave solutions of the dispersion relation obey the principle of superposition and we say that the particles which correspond to these waves are free or non-interacting. If we send these particles towards each other they will simply pass on through each other without scattering. Another recipe would be the Faddeev-Popov Lagrangian for the non-abelian gauge fields. But this would take too long for me to discuss here. Few lines suffice: The Lagrangian introduces the ghost field of ghost particles (unreal particles) to maintain gauge invariance and unitarity. Question: What are the key findings from the differential geometry of curves?
Answer: I'm not aware what the OP wants to know from this question. Differential geometry of curves involves the Frenet frame attached to the curve. The frame constitutes T , N , B which are orthogonal vectors attached to the curve in space and form equations called the Frenet formulas which allow us to derive mathematical measurements of the turning and twisting of a curve in say R 3 . Later on, this Frenet apparatus was generalized by Darboux to the theory of surfaces by introducing the method of moving frames. Cartan brought this moving frame method to full generality. The essential idea is simple. To each point of the object under study ( a curve, a surface, a Euclidean space itself,..) assign a frame. Then using orthonormal expansion express the rate of change of the frame in terms of the frame itself. This, of course, is just what the Frenet apparatus does in the case of a curve. The choice of the frame is very important. Later on, when connection forms come into picture, the subject gets more generalized and sophisticated. Ordinary derivative is replaced with covariant derivative. What a connection one-form tells us? Take a look at the equation. ω i j ( v ) = ∇ v E i . E j ( p ) The connection one-form ω i j is the initial rate at which E i rotates towards E j as p moves in the v direction. Connection forms form connection equations. These equations have a striking similarity to the Frenet formulas for curves. All books on differential geometry which go upto connection forms display this obvious relation between the geometry of curves and geometry of surfaces. Remember, covariant derivatives treat curved surfaces and hypersurfaces. Finally, the connection forms satisfy the famous Cartan structural equations. Everything comes under the domain of differential forms. One equation connects dual forms to connection forms. Dual forms describe the dual of the frame field. Other equation connects curvature forms to connection forms. This looks complicated and boring. But this forms the basis of the calculation of curvature of spacetime in general relativity for several types of metrics. Misner-Thorne-Wheeler's Gravitation leans heavily on connection forms and curvature forms via Cartan's equations. And all graduate level texts such as Wald's General Relativity discuss curvature in terms of connection forms besides other methods. Eventually, the approach goes to the level of Newman-Penrose null tetrad method which is something of a “dinosaur” in calculating curvature of “unfamiliar" metrics of spacetime. What starts as a simple differential geometry of a curve in space gives rise to a very heavy mathematical technology in sophisticated forms of general relativity and other related topics in theoretical physics.

Question: How does the language of QFT translate vague concepts into precise mathematical formulations?
Answer: Language of QFT is not vague. It is abstract. If you understand the formalism of QFT carefully, you will find that there are several results which encapsulate a physical idea and translate into a precise mathematical expression. Of course, when I say physical idea it means an idea which cannot be imagined in a classical manner. Take the following expression: G μ ν = ∂ μ A ν − ∂ ν A μ − i g [ A μ , A ν ] . This G μ ν is the non-abelian gauge field. The A μ are the vector potentials in terms of which the gauge field is expressed. The above expression tells you, roughly, how the gauge field G transforms when it is propagated from one point to the other. It is also called as the connection by physicists, because it connects the components of a vector at one point with its components at a nearby point. Here, we have the internal space rather than the curved spacetime of general relativity, where this rotation takes place. I said non-abelian gauge field above. This gauge field behaves differently from the abelian U ( 1 ) gauge field which is our familiar electromagnetic field F μ ν = ∂ μ A ν − ∂ ν A μ . What is the difference between these two expressions? The first one is the non-abelian gauge field, the second one is abelian. Mathematically, it means that the symmetry group of the first field is non-abelian, the symmetry group of the second field is abelian. Take the first gauge field as QCD, the interaction of quarks. Looking carefully at the above equations, we see that the third term in the first expression is absent in the second expression for the electromagnetic field. What it physically means? The third term − i g [ A μ , A ν ] reflects an important fact: the quanta of non-abelian gauge fields also interact with each other besides interacting with the quark field! The third term represents this interaction. For the electromagnetic field, this is absent thereby telling us that photons do not interact with each other than “mediating” the Dirac field (matter field). In other words, the quantity in the square brackets represents the interaction dynamics of the gauge particles among themselves. This term is called the commutator term. This is not a vague language, but one needs a careful study to obtain a physical picture from mathematical formalism and vice-versa. Without careful interpretation, the expression gets unintelligible. QFT is full of thousands of long, complex mathematical expressions. Hope this helps!

Question: Is theoretical physics a combination of philosophy and mathematics?
Answer: Theoretical physics is a combination of philosophy and mathematics with the necessary consistency in the formalism that can explain observed phenomena correctly or supplemented with predictive power of something which is testable in a reasonable sense. Einstein's general relativity explained the anomaly of the precession of the perihelion of Mercury which was an observed phenomenon, but it was not correctly explained in the Newtonian formalism of physics. Dirac's equation, while explaining the “motion” of an electron, predicted positron. These two examples fit the above requirements. However, theoretical physics also studies ideas which have been speculated and put on incorrect mathematical footing and therefore at variance with empirical evidence. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy is a single source which covers ideas of physics from Newtonian physics to quantum gravity under the broad idea of Philosophy of Physics and Mathematics. This is an important online source for theoretical physics and mathematics. Theoretical physics can also discuss ideas that lean more on philosophy or physical ideas than mathematics or lean more on mathematics than physical reality. Nordström gravity or Klein-Kaluza theory leaned more on mathematics than physics as conceivable at that time. But the mathematics did not encapsulate physical reality which is why they were discarded. Nevertheless, these come under theoretical physics as several other theories (Bohr's model, Bohm's theory) do. For example, Roger Penrose says ( Road to Reality p.873) “if you want to construct a QFT free of infinities, make your theory supersymmetric!”. No one has observed supersymmetry so far. But Penrose admits that it is one of the most elegant pieces of mathematics and has contributed to a very large number of modern fundamental theories, besides string theory (Witten used supersymmetry in his proof of positive mass theorem of general relativity in 1982). Witten's remark that “one may even wonder whether in the absence of local supersymmetry, the stability of general relativity could survive in a full quantum theory” looks very enigmatic. Yet, supersymmetry is physically not observed though it has worked well mathematically in theories which work well physically! At various stages, a complex and varying combination of physical insight, mathematics, rigor, philosophy and beauty play a fundamental role in the “lives” of these theories. Theoretical physics is a combination of every thing said above. Atiyah's remarks (on the occasion of Witten's Fields ceremony) on physics, mathematics, insight, reality, beauty and simplicity are something worth reading. Writing further would be boringly long here!

Question: Is "avoiding singularities" a big part of mathematics?
Answer: It is not even a small part of mathematics; it is a routine process. The day one starts learning about continuity and limits, one comes across points at which functions start behaving erratically. They blow up. There are beautiful results in complex analysis where singular points show up everywhere. There is a pole, essential singularity, removable singularity, etc. Contour integration avoids such points by “going around” such points or bypassing the points. Theoretical physics is marred with singularities. There is some concern about singularities in physical situations: Landau pole, pole in particle propagators, Schwarzchild exterior solution, singularity in black holes with blow-up of Riemann-Christoffel curvature tensor, Birkhoff theorem, etc. However, these situations are now well-known and extensively studied and there is no issue of what you say of “avoiding singularity”. If you want to avoid the singularity, just change the coordinate system. If the singularity persists, it is a physical singularity. Otherwise, its presence is coordinate-dependent and is not a real physical singularity.

Question: Do all mathematicians prefer simplicity over beauty in their equations/proofs, or vice versa? If not, why do some mathematicians prefer one over the other?
Answer: What is complex for you may be simple for the other. General relativity, for example, is one of the most beautiful and equally “simple” theories. This is what the experts say. However, what is simple is beautiful and vice-versa. But there is no specific classification of mathematical results in terms of beauty and simplicity. If the experts say this theory is much simpler than that theory, then we have to accept their verdict (even if we don't understand both!) For example, Simon Donaldson created his theory of differential topology of 4-manifolds in the 80s giving birth to what are called the Donaldson invariants. This theory borrowed ideas from Yang-Mills equations in mathematical physics. Though the Donaldson theory was conceptually elegant and beautiful, his two theorems embodying the theory had proofs which were formidably difficult by all standards. Few years later, Nathan Seiberg and Ed Witten came up with their own theory which provided an equivalent alternative to the Donaldson theory. This new theory is called the Seiberg-Witten theory. Contemporary mathematicians remarked that the new theory with its associated Seiberg-Witten equations is far simpler than its Donaldson counterpart. Some even said, the Seiberg-Witten invariants, as they are called, reduced the complexity of the earlier theory by half! Harvard mathematician Clifford Taubes said the computations were thousand times easier!! Both theories discovered/invented new techniques in differential topology of 4-manifolds and mathematical gauge theory. The new theory is said to be much simpler than its predecessor. Does that mean it is more beautiful than its predecessor? Yes, to some extent it is. It derives its force from differential geometry (an old subject) rather than differential topology (a 20th-century subject) in understanding 4-manifolds. For beginners, both might be impenetrable. The following book by Marcolli is very insightful for the ideas of the Seiberg-Witten theory. But it is a very difficult book. The author is one of the reputed collaborators of Fields Medalist Alain Connes.

Question: What does "intuition" mean in algebraic topology? Why do mathematicians need such an auxiliary concept for their research?
Answer: Intuition is at the base of algebraic topology. In fact, algebraic topology starts its life with real-life objects like circle, torus, sphere, etc. and studies their (topological) properties expressing them in terms of concepts of abstract algebra. How a ball is different from a donut is expressed in terms of curves drawn on the surface of these objects and watching them as they shrink to a point. In the case of a ball there is no issue: all curves shrink to a point, no matter where you draw them. But for the donut, this “shrinking to a point” property depends upon where you draw the curve. Some curves on donut will have to leave the surface to shrink to a point. Such properties are translated into ideas of linear algebra and group theory giving what is called the homotopy group and by other route the homology group. If two homology groups are isomorphic, this means the two topological spaces or manifolds can be deformed into each other. What is the first homology group, second homology group, etc. are all defined in terms of visualizable objects in real life in low dimensions. The above coffee cup and the donut are the same topologically. Here we go from real to abstract and form some set of ideas to build up abstract spaces and study them with algebraic tools to obtain further picture depending upon earlier known intuitive ideas. You don't have to worry what an eight-dimensional sphere looks like, or any dimension for that matter. Bott periodicity theorem of algebraic topology will tell you about S 8 in terms of lower dimensional spheres, roughly. Therefore, though the above is a rough characterization of ideas, the concept of intuition plays a dominant role in the development of algebraic topology. Closing this paragraph, an idea of a characteristic class being trivial (and this is an element of a cohomology group) for a vector bundle tells you that the bundle is trivial and has no twist anywhere. Doesn't this provide an intuition to the abstract idea of characteristic classes which classify bundles into different types? Those with twists and those without? It is this concept which distinguishes between a cyclinder strip and a Möbius strip! Therefore, calling intuition an auxiliary concept is absolutely incorrect way of looking at algebraic topology, even though I agree that intuition doesn't work all the way up into the most sophisticated and formidably difficult ideas in algebraic topology. Researchers, however, have the inside tract to comprehend such difficult ideas which exist in higher dimensions. And as algebraic topology is a very structured field, symmetry and periodicity do help in providing the necessary intuition.

Question: What is algebraic topology and how hard is it to learn?
Answer: Algebraic Topology tackles or studies topological features of spaces in terms of methods of abstract algebra. It sets up a bridge between algebra and topology. Algebraic topology is very hard. It depends upon what you want to learn. Generally, standard books on algebraic topology conclude with spectral sequences (Spanier Algebraic Topology). Spectral sequences are gadgets which are very difficult to understand unless one is thorough with (long) exact sequences and the results associated with them. There are several ramifications in algebraic topology like obstruction theory, topological K-theory, characteristic classes, fiber bundles, sheaf theory etc. Mathematical ideas such as characteristic classes, sheaves, sheaf cohomology, group cohomology, etc. were once (70 years ago) topics in algebraic topology . Now there are comprehensive books written on each one of them! Algebraic topology is as much vast as it is deep. Therefore, how hard is algebraic topology for you depends upon what topic you study and how deep you want to go. Hatcher wrote a book on spectral sequences describing several types of such sequences in different contexts. Now, again there are books on separate such sequences viz. Adams-Novikov spectral sequence. I'm really afraid to witness this level of “granularity” that exists in algebraic topology or any subject for that matter. Incidentally, American mathematician Mike Hopkins is said to be one of the leading experts in algebraic topology whose range of intellectual activities in algebraic topology is simply staggering. One of Hopkins’ notable PhD students is Jacob Lurie! Hope this helps.

Question: Can you describe a mathematical theorem without using any mathematical terms or symbols?
Answer: This would be impossible: theorem with no terms and symbols! But the Banach-Tarski theorem roughly fits the bill. Though the theorem is stated in mathematical terms of Euclidean space, bounded sets, rigid motions, non-measurable sets, etc., its intuitive description is pretty simple to understand: it is possible to cut a solid sphere into a finite number of pieces and to assemble these pieces to form two solid spheres the same size as the original sphere! Though this description is easy, the statement itself is counterintuitive. Another one comes to my mind: Jordan curve theorem: a simple closed curve in a plane determines two regions (the interior and the exterior region) and the curve is the common boundary of these two regions. This theorem is too obvious to be proved mathematically. But it has a proof which is difficult. Finally, several theorems in elementary number theory are described with the terms integers, rational numbers, real numbers, square of integers, etc. Although these are mathematical terms, they are too ubiquitous to be known to many. Statement of FLT is one such theorem.

Question: We have Gaussian curvature in the normal direction, so do we also have Gaussian curvature in the non normal direction?
Answer: No. The definition of Gaussian curvature demands the normal direction. The argument is simple. To investigate how much a surface curves is to look at the curvature of various curves on the surface. This is done via moving a tangent plane along the curve and looking at the normal vector to the tangent plane as to how much it tilts as we move along the curve. This is also done with the help of the Gauss map. This works along the same lines. Gauss map is the map from surface S to sphere S 2 . We have a surface patch σ : U → R 3 in S . Remember, the direction of the tangent plane to this surface patch σ is measured by the rate of change of N per unit area. Here the green area R is the image of σ under this map. This sends p to n ( p ) of S 2 . We focus on region R ⊆ U on S . We watch the amount by which n ( p ) varies the part σ ( R ) of the sphere by the area of the part n ( R ) of the sphere. Thus, the rate of change of n per unit area is given by the ratio. A ( n ( R ) ) A ( σ R ) Now the theorem linking these ideas says that as the region R shrinks to a point, this ratio becomes the absolute value of the Gaussian curvature of S. At every point of the argument above, we consider a normal direction to the surface in question. Therefore, there is no non-normal direction considered in the definition.

Question: What is the difficulty level of differential geometry for someone with a math background only (no physics)?

Still going higher up, one requires ideas from Yang-Mills theory (part of quantum field theory) to study differential geometry of 4-manifolds in terms of their invariants. However, all this takes you to a very sophisticated and formidable level of differential geometry. Marcolli's book is indispensable in understanding these ideas. Several theories in physics represent a blend of differential geometry, differential topology and physical ideas in an inseparable way.

Question: How would you intuitively explain the Atiyah-Singer Index Theorem to a layman?
Answer: It is not possible to explain the Atiyah-Singer index theorem to a layman. In this sense, the question appears to be ridiculous. It is not possible to explain this theorem even to math students who are foreign to the prerequisites (which is a very long list) needed to understand the technical statement of this theorem. In its most basic form the theorem says how to calculate the index of an elliptic operator D on a closed manifold in terms of topological invariants of the manifold. These topological invariants are the characteristic classes of the tangent bundle of the manifold M . So we have two indices, the analytic index and the topological index and the theorem proves that these two are equal. To atleast appreciate the theorem without understanding it, it is generally accepted that the theorem be studied in the particular cases which it reduces to. Even then, these particular cases are not familiar to most math students: Toeplitz index theorem, index of Dirac operator, Hirzebruch signature theorem, Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch theorem, etc.! One example which provides some intuition is the classical Gauss-Bonnet theorem. This theorem links geometry to topology, especially curvature to topology. As this question asks for intuition, I shall not write down the mathematical expression for the Gauss-Bonnet theorem. It has two sides: left side is the curvature K ( M ) and the right side is Euler characteristic χ ( M ) . This right side encodes topological information about the manifold. Further intuition provided by this result is, very roughly: too much curvature (geometry) will tear off (topology) the surface! Thus curvature and topology reside deeply in these indices as I mentioned above. They are sort of, “invisible to the naked eye”. Because, Atiyah-Singer index theorem replaces the tangent bundle by other bundles, the Gaussian curvature by higher-dimensional curvature forms, and replacing “general” operators by other elliptic differential operators associated with the bundle in question. Undeniably, this theorem is a very high point of geometric analysis of the twentieth century. Other case of interest is about Toeplitz operator where the index reduces to the winding number of a map from S 1 to C . But it requires some ideas of functional analysis. Three months back I bought the following book to study this theorem. I'm reading this book as per my convenience. Sir Amiya Mukherjee is an eminent mathematician and author who has written books on other topics too. The book is obviously difficult. But I'm in no hurry!

Question: Why are mathematical proofs so hard to understand and appreciate?
Answer: Everything requires practice. If one takes keen interest in understanding a difficult proof and works hard on it with familiarity with the proof's prerequisites, then the proof no longer remains hard to him/her. Of course, this is not a general rule. There are proofs that would take several years of study in order to understand them and appreciate them, even for those familiar with the necessary concepts. It takes deep thinking and indefatigably hard work to disentangle the complexity of the proof. Few years back, I had cherished the dream of understanding the Atiyah-Singer index theorem. I started studying partial differential equations, elliptic operators, elliptic complex, symbol of the differential operator, characteristic classes, Thom isomorphism theorem, etc. The list went on and on. Each of the above concepts was a sort of deep and subtle idea and synthesized subjects of partial differential equations, algebraic topology, analysis, operator algebras, etc. Over the top, there was the K-theory. Unfortunately, I could never bring all the above ideas into a coherent whole to understand the original proof of Atiyah-Singer. So, I shifted my focus to know how the theorem reduces in the particular cases of index theory: index theory on functions, index theory on de-Rham complex, etc., These particular cases turned out to be understandable! You can appreciate how the index theorem gives you Gauss-Bonnet theorem. No wonder, even today understanding the original proof has remained a dream only! Certain results in mathematics, which we generally call theorems, are inherently difficult even for mathematically oriented minds. In routine study, I need to read a (difficult) proof several times until I discern the logical structure and argument of the proof, assuming that I know the subject earlier. Finally, struggling to understand a proof is one of the most rewarding mental exercises in mathematics and is definitely worth the efforts, once you thoroughly understand the proof.

Question: How did Einstein know that Riemannian geometry was necessary for maintaining the equivalence principle in general relativity?
Answer: Connection between the physical idea of the equivalence principle and curved spacetime in general relativity is not very obvious, but it is interesting to know and is, in fact, very beautiful. In other words, how Riemannian geometry enters the principle of equivalence, is something to look for. Consider the differential equation: d 2 x t d s 2 + Γ t i j d x i d s d x j d s = 0 This is the equations of motion of a particle which moves along a world line. Roughly, this equation dictates the motion of a particle on a curved surface along the “straight line”. When the components of the metric tensor are constant, then Γ t i j is zero and the above equation in this case reduces to d 2 x t d s 2 = 0 which shows that the particle moves with a uniform velocity in a straight line. This is Newton's first law of motion. Note that this equation is in fact, ¨ x i + Γ i i j ˙ x l ˙ x k = F ……….(A) This is the Lagrange equations of motion and it clearly indicate the appearance of the Christoffel symbol in the equations of motion. If there are no forces, F i = 0 , and this equation is just the first equation and defines geodesic lines. Remember, here the differentiation is performed with respect to a time parameter t along the trajectory while in the first equation the differentiation is carried with respect to the arc length parameter s along the geodesics. This much you should know about Riemannian geometry. Now we enter the equivalence principle. A person in a lift falling freely in a gravitational field feels no such field inside the lift. Now put F i = 0 above in equation A. Then, ¨ x + Γ i i j ˙ x l ˙ x k = 0 This means that the acceleration of the particle, moving in the gravitational field, is proportional to the Christoffel symbols Γ . The vanishing of Christoffel symbol at a point means that we can choose a coordinate system in which the acceleration of the particle (here it is you) at a given point of the spacetime is zero, that is, the gravitational force acting on the particle vanishes at this point, or, in other words, by means of a coordinate transformation, the gravitational effects can be eliminated. But this happens only at a point and not in a finite region of spacetime. And this is your principle of equivalence! My own perspective on this is that, anyone who appreciates this reasoning which connects physical idea with geometry has understood the crux of the logic.
